title: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
directAnswer: This is interval-point-stabbing: each balloon is an interval [start,end], and one arrow at position x bursts every balloon whose interval contains x. Sort balloons by their END coordinate, then greedily fire an arrow at the end of the first unburst balloon — it pops every overlapping balloon for free. Count a new arrow only when a balloon starts strictly after the last arrow's position. O(n log n) for the sort, O(1) extra space. The answer is the number of arrows fired.

remember.pattern: Greedy interval point-stabbing — sort by END, shoot at end of current group
remember.formula:
points.sort(by end)
arrows = 1
arrowAt = points[0].end
for s, e in points[1:]:
    if s > arrowAt:          # this balloon starts after the arrow
        arrows += 1
        arrowAt = e          # new arrow at this balloon's end
return arrows
rules: **Sort by END coordinate, not start.** Shooting at the earliest end maximizes how many later balloons that single arrow can also catch.
Place the arrow at the **end** of the current balloon and reuse it for every balloon that starts at or before that position.
A new arrow is needed only when `start > arrowAt` — use **strict** `>` because touching endpoints (`[1,2]` and `[2,3]`) still share point 2 and burst together.
Start with `arrows = 1` (an empty array returns 0, so guard that first) — the first balloon always needs one arrow.
Sort by end using a **comparator that avoids `a-b` overflow** (values reach ±2³¹); use `Integer.compare` in Java.
whenToUse: Minimum points to 'stab' / cover all intervals (point-stabbing)
Fewest resources to handle every overlapping interval at once
Any 'one action clears a whole overlapping group' framing
Maximize reuse of a shared resource across overlapping ranges
antiSignals: You must MERGE overlaps into combined intervals → Merge Intervals, sort by start (LC 56)
You need the count of overlaps / rooms at a time → sweep-line or heap (Meeting Rooms II)
You delete the fewest intervals to make them disjoint → sort by end but COUNT keepers (LC 435)
Weighted intervals where each has a value → greedy fails, use DP
remember.takeaway: Sorting by END is the fingerprint of greedy interval problems where the earliest finisher is the safe choice. Here, an arrow at the earliest end stabs the most balloons; in Non-overlapping Intervals the earliest finisher leaves the most room. Same sort, same proof structure — recognize it and these problems collapse to a one-pass count.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize this as interval point-stabbing and know to sort by END (not start), plus whether you handle the touching-endpoints case with the correct strict comparison.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Sorting by start and getting a suboptimal arrow count, or using `>=` instead of `>` and firing an extra arrow for balloons that merely touch at an endpoint. Also `a[0]-b[0]` comparator overflow on extreme coordinates.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Justify the by-end sort with the exchange argument ('the earliest-ending balloon must be hit by some arrow; placing it at that end can only help later balloons'), and connect it to Non-overlapping Intervals as the same greedy family.

problemStatement:
There are some spherical balloons taped onto a flat wall that represents the XY-plane. The balloons are represented as a 2D integer array `points` where `points[i] = [x_start, x_end]` denotes a balloon whose **horizontal diameter** stretches between `x_start` and `x_end`. You do not know the exact y-coordinates of the balloons.

Arrows can be shot up **directly vertically** (in the positive y-direction) from different points along the x-axis. A balloon with `x_start` and `x_end` is **burst** by an arrow shot at `x` if `x_start <= x <= x_end`. There is no limit to the number of arrows that can be shot. A shot arrow keeps traveling up infinitely, bursting any balloons in its path.

Given the array `points`, return *the **minimum** number of arrows that must be shot to burst all balloons*.
understanding: Each balloon is a closed interval on the x-axis. An arrow at position x destroys every balloon whose interval contains x. We want the fewest arrow positions so that every balloon's interval contains at least one arrow position. Equivalently: the minimum number of points that 'stab' all the intervals. Balloons that share any common x can be burst by a single arrow.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the balloon intervals closed (endpoints inclusive)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — an arrow at x bursts a balloon when x_start <= x <= x_end, inclusive on both ends. That's why touching balloons like [1,2] and [2,3] can share an arrow at x=2.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can coordinates be negative or hit the 32-bit extremes?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, x ranges over the full int range. I'll avoid `a-b` subtraction in the comparator (it can overflow) and use Integer.compare instead.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the input sorted in any way?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, balloons come in arbitrary order. The first thing I'll do is sort them — by their end coordinate, which is the crux of the greedy.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The constraint says length ≥ 1, but defensively I'll return 0 for an empty input.

examples.explanation: After sorting by end: [1,6],[2,8],[7,12],[10,16]. Arrow at x=6 bursts [1,6] and [2,8]; arrow at x=12 bursts [7,12] and [10,16].
No two balloons overlap, so each needs its own arrow.
Arrow at x=2 bursts [1,2] and [2,3] (they touch at 2); arrow at x=4 bursts [3,4] and [4,5].

approaches.name: Brute Force — Try Arrow Positions Against All Balloons
approaches.whenToMention: Mention briefly to frame the problem ('naively, picking arrow positions and checking coverage is exponential'), then move to the greedy. Don't dwell — it's not implementable cleanly.
hints: Without a sorting insight, deciding the minimum set of stabbing points means searching over which balloons share an arrow — a set-cover-flavored search.
You could try every candidate arrow position (each balloon's endpoints) and greedily/recursively cover, but the naive search explodes combinatorially.
This is why we look for a structural property — sorting by end — that makes a simple greedy provably optimal.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Choosing which balloons each arrow handles, without the sorting structure, is a covering search whose naive form is exponential in the number of balloons — utterly impractical at n = 10⁵. Listed only to motivate the greedy.
approaches.explanation:
The literal reading of the problem — 'find the minimum set of x-positions such that every balloon contains one' — is a covering problem. Without exploiting structure, you'd be searching over subsets of balloons that can be grouped under a shared arrow, which blows up combinatorially.

**Why naive search fails.** With up to 10⁵ balloons, any approach that explores combinations of which balloons share an arrow is hopeless. Even a more disciplined recursion that, at each step, picks a balloon and branches over which other balloons to co-burst, has exponential worst-case behavior. There's no polynomial brute force worth writing here.

**Why it's still worth a sentence.** Naming the brute-force framing — 'this is essentially a minimum point-cover over intervals' — signals to the interviewer that you understand the problem's true nature before you reveal the trick. It also sets up the payoff: interval problems with this shape almost always have a greedy that sorting unlocks, so the natural next question is *what should we sort by?*

**The pivot.** The moment you sort the balloons by their end coordinate, the search collapses: a single left-to-right pass with one running 'last arrow position' computes the optimum. That transformation from exponential search to linear greedy is the entire lesson of this problem.
approaches.insight: When the brute force for an interval problem is set-cover-flavored and exponential, that's the cue to find a sort order that makes a greedy optimal. The candidate that recognizes 'this smells like interval greedy' and asks 'sort by start or end?' is already most of the way to the answer.

approaches.name: Greedy — Sort by End, Shoot at Earliest End (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Lead with 'sort by end, fire at the end of the first balloon, reuse it for everything that overlaps'.
hints: Think about the balloon that ends earliest. Some arrow must burst it. Where should that arrow go to also help as many other balloons as possible?
Put the arrow exactly at that earliest end. Any balloon whose start is at or before that position is also burst for free. Only when a balloon starts strictly after your arrow do you need a new one.
So: sort by end, fire at points[0].end, and walk forward — increment the arrow count and reset the arrow position only when a balloon's start exceeds the current arrow position.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting dominates at O(n log n). The single pass that counts arrows is O(n). Aside from the sort (which can be in place), only a couple of scalars are used → O(1) extra space (O(1) ignoring sort's recursion, or O(log n) for the sort's stack depending on implementation).
approaches.explanation:
Model each balloon as a closed interval `[start, end]`; an arrow at `x` bursts a balloon iff `start <= x <= end`. We want the fewest arrow positions covering every interval — classic **interval point-stabbing**, solved by a greedy that sorts by **end** coordinate.

**The greedy choice and why end, not start.** Consider the balloon that finishes earliest (smallest `end`). *Some* arrow has to burst it, and that arrow must be placed at a position `<= end`. Among all such positions, placing it exactly at `end` is weakly best: it's the rightmost legal spot, so it can also reach the most balloons that start later. Formally, by an **exchange argument**, in any optimal solution we can slide the arrow that bursts the earliest-ending balloon rightward to that balloon's `end` without losing any coverage — so there's always an optimal solution that fires at the earliest end. Sorting by `start` doesn't give this guarantee: a balloon with a small start but huge end could swallow the decision and force suboptimal grouping.

**The single pass.** After sorting by end, fire the first arrow at `points[0].end` and set `arrowAt = points[0].end`, with `arrows = 1`. Scan the rest: for each balloon, if its `start <= arrowAt`, the current arrow already pierces it (because we sorted by end, its end is ≥ arrowAt, and its start ≤ arrowAt means arrowAt lies inside it) — do nothing. The instant a balloon has `start > arrowAt`, the current arrow misses it entirely, so we must fire a fresh arrow; we place it at *this* balloon's end and bump the count. Each balloon is examined once, so the scan is linear.

**Why the comparison must be strict (`>`).** The intervals are closed, so two balloons that merely *touch* — `[1,2]` and `[2,3]` — both contain the point `2` and can be burst by one arrow. If we used `start >= arrowAt` to decide a new arrow is needed, we'd wrongly fire a second arrow for the touching balloon. Using strict `start > arrowAt` correctly treats touching as overlapping. This single character is the most common bug on this problem.

**Why sort comparison must avoid overflow.** Coordinates span the full 32-bit range down to `-2³¹` and up to `2³¹ − 1`. A naive comparator `return a[1] - b[1];` can overflow (e.g. a large positive minus a large negative wraps to a negative-looking result), corrupting the sort. Use `Integer.compare(a[1], b[1])` in Java; Python's `sort(key=lambda p: p[1])` has arbitrary precision and is safe. With a correct sort and the strict comparison, the pass yields the provably minimum arrow count.
approaches.insight: This is the twin of Non-overlapping Intervals: both sort by end because the earliest finisher is the 'safe' greedy pick. Here, firing at the earliest end stabs the maximal overlapping group; there, keeping the earliest finisher leaves maximal room. When you see 'minimum X to handle all overlapping intervals', reach for sort-by-end and an exchange-argument proof.

dryRun.intro: Sort by end → [1,6],[2,8],[7,12],[10,16]. Fire at the first end, reuse while balloons start ≤ arrowAt.

code.python:
def findMinArrowShots(self, points: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    if not points:
        return 0

    points.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])      # sort by END

    arrows = 1
    arrow_at = points[0][1]               # fire at the earliest end
    for start, end in points[1:]:
        if start > arrow_at:              # strict: touching balloons share an arrow
            arrows += 1
            arrow_at = end
    return arrows

java.explanation: Sort by END coordinate; Integer.compare avoids overflow that a[1]-b[1] would cause.
Greedy: place the first arrow at the earliest end so it catches the most later balloons.
STRICT >: touching endpoints share an arrow, so only a true gap forces a new one.
New arrow goes at this balloon's end — the new rightmost reachable point.

python.explanation: Sort by END; Python ints are arbitrary precision so no overflow.
Fire the first arrow at the earliest-ending balloon's end.
Strict comparison so [1,2] and [2,3] (touching at 2) share one arrow.
Reposition the conceptual arrow to this balloon's end.

edgeCases.behavior: Single balloon → arrows initialized to 1, loop body never runs → 1.
Touching at 2; start 2 is NOT > arrowAt 2 → one arrow.
Extreme coords; Integer.compare keeps the sort correct where a-b would overflow → two arrows.

pitfalls: Sorting by start instead of end — produces wrong (often too-many) arrow counts.
Using >= instead of > — fires an extra arrow for balloons that merely touch.
Comparator a[1] - b[1] overflowing at int extremes — use Integer.compare.
Initializing arrows to 0 and forgetting the first balloon always needs one (guard empty input separately).

commonMistakes: Sorting by start coordinate instead of end.
Using >= rather than strict > when deciding a new arrow is needed (touching balloons).
Comparator overflow from a[1] - b[1] at the 32-bit extremes.
Returning 0 for a non-empty input by initializing the arrow count wrong.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sorting by start instead of end
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The greedy proof relies on the earliest-ENDING balloon: its end is the optimal arrow position. Sorting by start can group balloons that don't actually share a common point optimally, inflating the count.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: points.sort(key=lambda p: p[0])   # by start — wrong greedy
commonMistakesDetailed.good: points.sort(key=lambda p: p[1])   # by end — earliest finisher first

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using >= instead of strict >
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Intervals are closed, so [1,2] and [2,3] both contain x=2 and burst with one arrow. With >=, a balloon starting exactly at arrowAt is treated as a miss, firing a needless extra arrow.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparator overflow at int extremes
commonMistakesDetailed.why: x can be -2³¹ or 2³¹-1. The subtraction a[1] - b[1] overflows (e.g. 2³¹-1 minus -2³¹ wraps negative), so Arrays.sort orders elements incorrectly.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: Arrays.sort(points, (a, b) -> a[1] - b[1]);   // overflow at extremes

followupVariations.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
followupVariations.hint: Same sort-by-end greedy; count KEEPERS (survivors) and return n − keepers.

followupVariations.title: Merge Intervals
followupVariations.hint: Different goal — combine overlaps; sort by START and sweep, extending the running end.

followupVariations.title: Meeting Rooms II
followupVariations.hint: Count max concurrent overlaps with a min-heap of end times or a sweep line.

followupVariations.title: Maximum Length of Pair Chain
followupVariations.hint: Activity-selection again: sort by end, greedily chain non-overlapping pairs.

patternNote: Greedy interval point-stabbing. Recognize it when one action (an arrow, a point) must cover every overlapping interval and you want the fewest actions. Sort by END and shoot at the earliest end — the same exchange-argument greedy behind Non-overlapping Intervals and Maximum Length of Pair Chain. Contrast with Merge Intervals (sort by start) and Meeting Rooms II (count concurrency).
